hints: Remember the Brønsted-Lowry test is very specific, a base must accept a proton ($\text{H}^+$) to form its conjugate acid.
Look for the reaction where $\text{NH}_3$ turns into the ammonium ion, $\text{NH}_4^+$, because that gain of $\text{H}^+$ is the key clue.
Check where the $\text{H}^+$ comes from and rule out reactions where ammonia loses $\text{H}^+$, attacks carbon, or is oxidised instead.
walkthrough:
**Recall what a Brønsted-Lowry base does**

A Brønsted-Lowry base is a proton acceptor. It takes an $\text{H}^+$ from an acid and forms its conjugate acid.

For ammonia the test is:
$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+$$

**Track what happens to nitrogen in each reaction**

Look at the nitrogen containing product to see if $\text{NH}_3$ gained $\text{H}^+$, lost $\text{H}^+$, or did something else entirely.

In option B we get $\text{NH}_4^+$, which means $\text{NH}_3$ has gained a proton.

**Confirm the proton source and conclude**

In B, water and carbon dioxide together provide $\text{H}^+$ via carbonic acid, so ammonia accepts $\text{H}^+$ to give ammonium hydrogencarbonate:
$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{HCO}_3^-$$
This is classic base behaviour, so this is the Brønsted-Lowry base reaction.

options.A: Incorrect. Here $\text{NH}_3$ attacks the carbon in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. It is acting as a nucleophile (a Lewis base donating its lone pair to carbon), not as a Brønsted-Lowry base accepting $\text{H}^+$.
options.B: Correct. $\text{NH}_3$ gains a proton to form $\text{NH}_4^+$ in $(\text{NH}_4)\text{HCO}_3$. Accepting $\text{H}^+$ is exactly the Brønsted-Lowry base definition, with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ plus $\text{CO}_2$ acting as the proton source.
options.C: Incorrect. Here $\text{NH}_3$ is converted to $\text{NH}_2^-$ in $\text{NaNH}_2$, so it has lost $\text{H}^+$. Losing a proton is Brønsted-Lowry acid behaviour, the opposite of what is asked.
options.D: Incorrect. This is a redox combustion reaction. Nitrogen changes oxidation number from -3 in $\text{NH}_3$ to 0 in $\text{N}_2$, so ammonia is acting as a reducing agent, not as a proton acceptor.
